body: Confirmed, sort of. I get a traceback, not a segfault, but it's a `RecursionError`, and it's not impossible that could cause a segfault on some platforms. (I used a Mac.)
I can confirm that this does unfortunately lead to a segfault on Ubuntu 18.04 (and other Linux systems as well I presume).

Also confirmed as a segfault on my 18.04 system. We call `sys.setrecursionlimit(2 ** 14)`, and if I change it to `2 ** 13` I get a RecursionError on my machine.

I am somewhat surprised by this, though. 2 ** 14 is 16384, which is just not a very big number.

> I am somewhat surprised by this, though. 2 ** 14 is 16384, which is just not a very big number.

Aha:
```
$ ulimit -s
8192
```
That is also not a very big number. So in addition to fixing the actual bug, we should reduce our recursion limit, probably. (Or call setrlimit, I guess)
Can python be compiled with split stacks? https://gcc.gnu.org/wiki/SplitStacks

> Can python be compiled with split stacks? https://gcc.gnu.org/wiki/SplitStacks

Out of scope for us, in any case.
(Also probably not?)

> > Can python be compiled with split stacks? https://gcc.gnu.org/wiki/SplitStacks
> 
> Out of scope for us, in any case.
> (Also probably not?)

I was mentioning split stacks since I think that would effectively remove the issue with running out of stack space causing a sigsegv since split stacks basically allow recursion until the heap is exhausted.

That doesn't seem particularly useful in this case since it would just delay the stack overflow, and it would probably make things worse for the system as mypy would eat up huge amounts of memory. As @msullivan said above, we should fix two things for this bug:

- Remove the infinite recursion in your test case above
- Avoid setting recursion limits higher than the rlimit for recursion, so that mypy doesn't segfault if it hits runaway recursion.
I think this is a duplicate of https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/5171, but I am going to close that instead since this one has more context and a simpler repro.

issue.title: Fix __getattr__ and operators related infinite recursion
__getattr__ returning self type results in RecursionError in overloaded contexts
issue.body:
The following code (`foo.pyi`):

```python
from typing import Any, Callable, overload

class T:
    def __getattr__(self, item: Any) -> T: ...

@overload
def f(f: Callable[..., Any], t: str = ...) -> Callable[...,  T]: ...
@overload
def f(f: str = ...) -> Callable[[Callable[..., Any]], Callable[..., T]]: ...
```

when used with current master

```
$ mypy --version                      
mypy 0.730+dev.aaad048cf6f88280f4295865882888b7721dacdb
```

with default options 

```
mypy --show-traceback foo.py
```
results in `RecursionError`

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/zero323/anaconda3/bin/mypy", line 10, in <module>
    sys.exit(console_entry())
...
RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded while calling a Python object
foo.pyi:6: : note: use --pdb to drop into pdb
```


with repeated following calls:

```
  File "/path/to/anaconda3/lib/python3.7/site-packages/mypy/subtypes.py", line 152, in _is_subtype
    ignore_promotions=self.ignore_promotions)
  File "/path/to/anaconda3/lib/python3.7/site-packages/mypy/subtypes.py", line 95, in is_subtype
    ignore_promotions=ignore_promotions))
  File "/path/to/anaconda3/lib/python3.7/site-packages/mypy/types.py", line 667, in accept
    return visitor.visit_instance(self)
  File "/path/to/anaconda3/lib/python3.7/site-packages/mypy/subtypes.py", line 232, in visit_instance
```

The problem disappears if:

- We remove `__getattr__`. Other dunders with the same signature, for example

      class T:
          def __getitem__(self, item: Any) -> T: ...

  seem to work fine.

- We change return type of `__getattr__`, for example:

      class T:
           def __getattr__(self, item: Any) -> str: ...

- We remove any of the overloaded `f`. Either 

      def f(f: Callable[..., Any], t: str = ...) -> Callable[...,  T]: ...

  or

      def f(f: str = ...) -> Callable[[Callable[..., Any]], Callable[..., T]]: ...

  alone, works just fine.

- We change return type of the first overloaded `f`, for example to:

      def f(f: Callable[..., Any], t: str = ...) -> Callable[...,  int]: ...

  or even other `Generic` of `T`:

      def f(f: Callable[..., Any], t: str = ...) -> List[T]: ..

- We make `t` obligatory in both overloaded definitions, or remove it completely from the second one.

The same code causes segmentation fault with the latest PyPi release:

```
$ mypy --show-traceback foo.pyi
[1]    1530 segmentation fault  mypy --show-traceback foo.pyi
```

so it might be (?) related to #6579.
